People feel like the economy is rigged because over the last four decades the role of corporations and the laws that regulate intellectual property rights, contracts, trade unions, monopolies, and more have been changed (or have seen the agencies responsible for enforcing those laws de-funded and the laws thusly de-fanged) at the behest of wealthy individuals and corporations--who donate and lobby profusely--in ways that erect barriers to entry for small businesses, low-income families, outsider political parties, labor unions, etc as well as making it more difficult for the average person to influence their employer and their government, or even to have their voice heard on economic issues.

The result has been less responsive government, less market competition, less bargaining power for workers, stagnating wages, higher unemployment, rampant underemployment, "labor flexibility" (which has devastated the family), precipitous drops in education funding, dysfunctional government, partisan gridlock, and ever increasing inequality of income and of wealth (which only serves to increase the disparity between political power among the elite and among the masses).

Look at the research from Gilens and Page, of Stanford, who used data from (IIRC) 1981-2002 (pre-citizens united) to show that even before that disastrous decision, "the preferences of average people seem to have a minuscule, near zero, statistically insignificant effect on public policy."

One can safely imagine that any shadow of correlation between the preferences of average people and the decisions of our legislatures has faded or vanished entirely by now.

This isn't the fault of all successful people, or even an accusation that any have done anything intentionally malicious. The exact same motivations of self-interest that we all act under have lead to an effect greater than the sum of its parts in economic terms. One firm, one person, lobbying for one rule change is not doing something morally wrong, but a system that allows this over and over again is bound to create an economy that is biased towards the holders of capital, and against labor.

I don't think it's correct to blame the current economic conditions all on lobbying and money in politics. I believe that other factors, such as automation of factories and flight of jobs overseas, have played a larger role.

But regardless, I don't think things have changed as much as you would like to believe. Forty years ago, someone who stayed in a factory job their entire life was doomed to a pretty miserable economic existence. If you don't have a fancy formal education then you have to become an entrepreneur to get ahead. So many people who have come to this country barely speaking the language, who have opened their own businesses and have prospered. I don't see anything stopping someone from doing that today.

Forty years ago, if someone stayed in their factory job their whole life, they would most likely end up in a supervisory position making pretty good money. Even if they didn't they would almost definitely be able to be a sole provider for their family. I work in a factory job currently. All promotions are blocked by requiring a four year degree. I make so little that my wife also has to work a job just so we can stay afloat. Between her working and me working overtime I don't have the time to go to school to get the degree I need to get a promotion. I could look for another job but since I've never had a supervisory role, I would likely make even less than I make right now.

But the "flight of jobs overseas" is just another symptom of this systemic problem. Why is the tax code structured the way it is? Why are businesses not only allowed to do this, but rewarded for doing so? If the people's will was reflected in public policy, this would not be so.

As for changes in the last 40 years:

The role of corporations

The period from the 1980s to the present has been marked by a major shift away from a broad view of stakeholder interests to an almost exclusive focus on shareholder value. Galbraith’s countervailing powers had in fact begun to break down by the 1970s. Declining union membership gradually reduced the influence of big laboron corporate managers. Corporations hastened the trend by closing factories in the old manufacturing belt of the Northeast and Midwest, where unions were strong, shifting production to Sun Belt states that had long anti-union traditions. The old manufacturing areas became known as the Rust Belt.

Countervailing power weakened further as academics and others began to attack government antitrust and regulatory policies as misguided. They called for deregulation and increasingly placed government itself under scrutiny. Instead of working in the public interest, many argued, government practiced interest-group politics. Bureaucrats had their own interests–larger budgets, more authority, more employees–which had little to do with the public interest. Ronald Reagan, the popular president from 1981 to 1989, epitomized this new view when he famously said government wasn’t the solution, it was the problem.

Academics came to the rescue of corporations, or so it seemed, with new theories of what corporate managers should do. Instead of catering to the interests of various stakeholders, as they had done in the good old days of the postwar era, managers would best serve owners and society in general, the academics argued, by single-mindedly working to maximize shareholder value. The stakeholder view was complicated; actions that are in the interests of some stakeholders may be counter to the interests of others. Higher wages may mean lower profits, and lower wages may mean higher profits.
